name: Mykhailo Titov
lead: I build across the stack — from a Verilog error-correcting decoder and a mesh-routing protocol to Spring Boot APIs and Python agents on top of LLMs.
meta_description: Mykhailo Titov — software engineer and ICT student in Bratislava. Case studies in Java/Spring Boot, React, network protocols, Verilog and AI automation.

bio: I study Information and Communication Technologies at STU FEI in Bratislava and Computer Science in parallel at Dnipro University of Technology.

I like knowing what happens underneath an interface, so my projects go deep in different directions: a mesh-routing protocol with 167 passing tests, a Verilog decoder, Java backends with JWT and WebSockets, and Python agents built on LLM APIs.

Right now I’m building Python agents on top of GPT and Claude APIs, tools for evaluating LLM output, and n8n automation pipelines. I also team up at hackathons: RAKATHON 2026, Huawei Seeds for the Future and the STU Ideathon, where my team placed 3rd.

projects.title: Task Tracker
projects.outcome: A project workspace with 35 REST endpoints and a drag-and-drop widget dashboard
projects.subtitle: Projects, tasks, time tracking and analytics in one workspace.
projects.summary: A full-stack workspace for projects, tasks, time tracking, analytics and customizable widgets, with a Spring Boot backend and a React frontend.

media.alt: Task Tracker overview: a widget dashboard with a focus timer, upcoming reminders, a focus-trend chart, project progress and a tasks-by-status chart.

gallery.alt: Analytics page with completed tasks and focus hours over a week, a tasks-by-status donut and a project-progress bar chart.
gallery.caption: Analytics: completed tasks vs. focus hours, status breakdown and project progress.

gallery.alt: Project details page listing tasks with status, priority, due date and tag columns and filters.
gallery.caption: Project details: filterable task list with inline status changes.

projects.media_note: Screenshots of the real React frontend running locally with the project’s demo account; API responses were filled with seed-style demo data for the capture.
projects.problem: Tasks, time entries and project progress are easier to understand when they live in one place. The goal was a single workspace where planning, focus time and progress feed the same dashboard.
implementation: JWT authentication plus CRUD APIs for projects, tasks, reminders and widgets — 35 endpoints documented with OpenAPI/Swagger.
Seven React screens: overview, projects with task board, calendar, analytics, time tracker, widget studio and settings.
Time tracking with an active-session model, and analytics endpoints for KPIs, productivity, status breakdown and project progress.
A drag-and-resize widget grid with a template marketplace and a draft → validate → publish flow.
Flyway migrations, H2 for local runs, PostgreSQL in Docker Compose, and integration tests for auth, projects and tasks.
projects.results: A complete, runnable application: one `docker compose up` starts PostgreSQL, the backend and the frontend. Stored “Java logic” in widgets is validated but never executed on the server, and “Generate with AI” is a rule-based UI mock.
projects.learning: Designing the widget system taught me to keep extensibility safe: user-defined content is stored and validated, but the server never runs it.
cv_points: Spring Boot 3 + JWT backend: 35 REST endpoints, Flyway migrations, integration tests.
React dashboard with drag-and-resize widgets, analytics charts and time tracking.

projects.title: KIZUNA v2
projects.outcome: A self-healing IPv6 mesh-routing protocol, validated on a 12-node Docker lab
projects.subtitle: Keeps a mesh network routing when links and nodes fail.
projects.summary: An adaptive mesh-routing protocol for unstable autonomous devices: neighbor discovery, link evaluation, gradual neighbor admission, primary and backup paths, and resilience modes — with a Docker lab and a web simulator to make it visible.

media.alt: Map of the default KIZUNA field scenario: two gateways in opposite corners, seven routers, two modules and two standby routers spread over a 1600 by 900 metre area.

projects.media_note: Node positions and roles are taken from the repository’s simulator/scenario.json. Test count from running pytest on the public repository in October 2026.
projects.problem: When links are unstable and nodes disappear, a static route stops working. KIZUNA explores how autonomous devices can discover each other, decide which links to trust, share topology and keep traffic moving as conditions degrade.
implementation: A binary packet envelope (magic “KIZU”) and six core messages: HELLO, LSA, DATA, SOS, LAYER and PREDICT, sent over UDP/IPv6 multicast.
Gradual neighbor admission with repeated proof of identity, so the mesh doesn’t instantly trust every device it hears.
A link-state database and routing engine that keep a primary and a backup path, plus a relay advisor that prefers capable, under-used nodes.
Four resilience layers (normal, degraded, emergency, survival) and four traffic classes, so control and SOS traffic survive while bulk traffic is shed first.
A 12-container Docker lab with reproducible fault injection (tc netem, container stop/start), gateway failover, and a web dashboard of nodes, links and paths.

facts.label: Packet header
facts.code:
struct "!4sBBIdHI"
magic       4s   "KIZU"
version     B
msg_type    B
sequence    I
timestamp   d
node_id_len H
payload_len I

projects.results: Public repository with the protocol core, a reproducible 12-node lab and a dashboard. The test suite (167 tests) passes on a clean checkout. The roadmap now turns the lab protocol into a real Linux overlay with a `kiz0` TUN interface.
projects.learning: Separating the protocol core from the simulator, collector and dashboard made each layer testable on its own — and made it possible to boot the daemon on a real node without the simulator.
cv_points: Binary protocol over UDP/IPv6 multicast with neighbor admission and backup paths.
12-node Docker lab with fault injection and gateway failover; 167 passing tests.

projects.title: Appointment System
projects.outcome: A clinic booking system where every appointment opens its own doctor–patient chat
projects.subtitle: Role-based clinic bookings with appointment-linked chat.
projects.summary: A role-based clinic application for patient bookings, doctor schedules, administration and appointment-linked messaging.

media.alt: Appointment chat: a thread per booking on the left, and a conversation that starts with the doctor's automatic message for the booked time.

gallery.alt: Doctor portal dashboard with counters for today, this week, completed appointments and chat threads, a recent-appointments table and quick actions.
gallery.caption: Doctor portal: daily counters, recent bookings with status, quick actions.

projects.media_note: Screenshots of the real React + TypeScript frontend running locally as the seeded doctor account; API responses were filled with seed-style demo data for the capture.
projects.problem: A booking involves three parties: a patient choosing a time, a doctor with a schedule, and staff who oversee everything. Messages about the visit usually end up in a separate channel, disconnected from the booking itself.
implementation: Patient, doctor and admin roles, each with its own pages and permissions enforced by Spring Security and JWT.
Free slots generated from each doctor’s weekly schedule, with conflict checks before a booking is saved.
Every booking automatically creates a chat thread and a first message from the doctor’s template ({doctorName}, {date}, {time}…).
Realtime chat over STOMP / SockJS with a REST fallback, plus Swagger docs and service tests for auth, doctors and appointments.
projects.results: Runnable locally with an H2 database and seeded accounts; the configuration is ready for PostgreSQL. It is a software project, not a deployed clinical service.
projects.learning: Keeping booking rules on the backend — slot generation, conflict checks, role checks — kept the three interfaces simple and consistent.

card_media.alt: Doctor portal dashboard with counters for today, this week, completed appointments and chat threads, a recent-appointments table and quick actions.

cv_points: Slot generation from doctor schedules with conflict checks; three user roles.
Each booking opens a STOMP/WebSocket chat with the doctor’s automatic message.

projects.title: ProstaPaper
projects.outcome: A RAKATHON prototype that fills a urologist’s REDCap documentation from his records — and flags the errors it finds
projects.subtitle: Reads clinical records, fills REDCap and flags inconsistencies.
projects.summary: Built by our team at RAKATHON 2026 in Brno, billed as the world’s largest AI hackathon against cancer. A urologist treating prostate cancer needed a tool that reads his records, compares them, fills the hospital’s REDCap documentation — and points out errors and contradictions in the records.

media.alt: Illustration: a doctor's record on the left with highlighted passages, and the proposed REDCap form on the right, where one field is flagged because two sources disagree.

projects.media_note: Illustration with generic placeholder fields. No patient data is shown anywhere on this site.
projects.problem: A urologist treating prostate cancer copies information from his own reports, notes and diagrams into the hospital’s REDCap registry by hand. It takes time, and mistakes in the source records travel straight into the database.
implementation: Reads the doctor’s records — reports, notes and tumour diagrams — and extracts the value each REDCap field needs.
Compares the documents with each other, so every value is checked against all of its sources.
Flags errors and contradictions in the records and shows the doctor exactly where they are. This was the key feature.
Fills the REDCap form as a proposal: nothing is saved until the doctor reviews and confirms it.
Designed to run on hospital-controlled servers, so documents never leave the institution.
projects.results: Team prototype presented at RAKATHON 2026 in Brno. Using it on real patient records would need clinical validation and an approved hospital deployment.
projects.learning: In medical documentation, catching mistakes in the source records matters as much as filling the form — and the doctor has to stay in control of every value.
cv_points: Reads a urologist’s records, cross-checks values and fills REDCap forms.
Flags contradictions in the records for the doctor before anything is saved.

projects.title: Hybrid SEC-DED Decoder
projects.outcome: An extended Hamming (8,4) decoder in Verilog that corrects single-bit errors and flags double-bit ones
projects.subtitle: Error correction in Verilog, from codeword to bit-error rate.
projects.summary: Extended Hamming (8,4) encoding and decoding in Verilog, reliability-based hybrid correction logic, and a BPSK + AWGN simulation setup for comparing hard and hybrid decoding.

media.alt: Extended Hamming (8,4) codeword with eight bit cells. Bit 5 is flipped; the syndrome 101 points to position 5 and the overall parity check confirms a single, correctable error.

projects.media_note: Textbook illustration of extended Hamming (8,4) — not the project’s measured results.
projects.problem: A noisy channel can flip transmitted bits. This research connects the theory of error-correcting codes with a hardware implementation and an experiment that compares decoding strategies.
implementation: An extended Hamming (8,4) SEC-DED encoder and decoder written in Verilog.
A custom bit layout that maps syndrome values directly to bit positions.
Reliability checks and hybrid correction logic on top of hard-decision decoding.
A BPSK + AWGN simulation for measuring bit-error rate across an Eb/N0 sweep.
projects.results: Research in progress. The source and measured BER curves are not public yet.
projects.learning: Testbenches and controlled experiments are how a decoder proves it is correct — and show exactly where it starts to fail.
cv_points: Extended Hamming (8,4) encoder and decoder in Verilog with hybrid correction.
BPSK + AWGN simulation comparing bit-error rates across an Eb/N0 sweep.

projects.title: Study Group
projects.outcome: A study-group app with realtime chat, shared tasks and files, built for Google Cloud
projects.subtitle: Chat, tasks and shared files for study groups.
projects.summary: A study-group web app with realtime chat, shared tasks, file resources, member roles and notifications, with a documented Google Cloud deployment.

media.alt: Architecture: a React single-page app talks to a Spring Boot API over REST and a WebSocket chat channel; the API stores data in Cloud SQL PostgreSQL and files in Cloud Storage, and both run on Cloud Run.

projects.media_note: Architecture drawn from the repository’s README and deployment configuration.
projects.problem: Study groups scatter discussion, tasks and materials across different apps. The idea was one group workspace where a chat message can point straight at a task or a file.
implementation: Groups with member roles, task CRUD with deadlines and priorities, and file resources linked to tasks.
Realtime chat over a plain WebSocket endpoint with typing events, online status and task/resource events.
Email + password and Google OAuth2 sign-in, both issuing JWTs.
Deployment configuration for Cloud Build → Cloud Run, Cloud SQL and a Cloud Storage bucket for files.
projects.results: Public source with local startup and cloud deployment instructions. This site doesn’t claim a production deployment is currently online.
projects.learning: Mixing request/response APIs with realtime events forced clear rules about what the server broadcasts and when the client refetches.
cv_points: Realtime WebSocket chat linked to group tasks and shared files.
JWT + Google OAuth2; deployment config for Cloud Run, Cloud SQL and Storage.

projects.title: Job Hunter Agent
projects.outcome: An agent that scans five job boards, scores each listing with Azure OpenAI and shortlists the 7+/10 ones
projects.subtitle: Turns a noisy job feed into a scored shortlist.
projects.summary: A Python pipeline that collects job listings, filters low-signal posts, scores relevance with Azure OpenAI and logs results to Google Sheets.

media.alt: Pipeline: listings from Profesia.sk, Worki.sk, LinkedIn, Jobs.sk and Reddit are filtered, scored 0 to 10 by Azure OpenAI, and written to a shortlist sheet (score 7 or more) and a full log sheet.

projects.media_note: Pipeline drawn from the repository’s README and source.
projects.problem: Job feeds are full of duplicates, “for hire” posts, discussions and senior-only roles. Reading all of it by hand doesn’t scale.
implementation: Collectors for Profesia.sk, Worki.sk, LinkedIn, Jobs.sk and Reddit.
Deterministic pre-filters for candidate posts, general discussions and strong seniority mismatches — before any model call.
Azure OpenAI scores each remaining listing from 0 to 10; listings scoring 7 or more go to the shortlist.
Two Google Sheets views (shortlist and full log), deduplication via a processed-jobs file, and a cron schedule every six hours.
projects.results: Public Python project. It runs on a schedule with configured API keys; Gmail reply checking is currently disabled, and it never applies to jobs on its own.
projects.learning: Cheap deterministic filters in front of the model cut both cost and noise — the model only judges listings that could plausibly fit.
cv_points: Collects listings from five job boards and filters noise before any model call.
Azure OpenAI scores each listing 0–10; anything 7+ goes to a Google Sheets shortlist.

projects.title: Video Editing Automation
projects.outcome: A Claude Code skill that turns a voiceover into a captioned DaVinci Resolve edit
projects.subtitle: From a narration recording to a first cut in DaVinci Resolve.
projects.summary: An AI-assisted editing workflow packaged as a Claude Code skill: transcription, silence and filler trimming, captions, clip and sound selection, colour grade and a DaVinci Resolve timeline.

media.alt: Pipeline: voiceover, transcribe, trim silence and fillers, captions, match clips and sound, colour grade, DaVinci Resolve timeline, draft render.

projects.media_note: Pipeline drawn from the repository’s scripts and README.
projects.problem: Turning a narration into a fast-cut, captioned video takes dozens of small, repetitive editing decisions.
implementation: Transcription and cut planning that trims silence and filler words without cutting a word in half.
Synced captions, clip and sound-effect selection from a local media library, with generated frames as a fallback.
Two style profiles (faceless visual essay, talking-head/screen demo) with overlays for one-off tweaks.
DaVinci Resolve automation for tracks, captions, grade and render, plus timeline validation and a local dashboard for parallel builds.
projects.results: Public repository with an environment checker and setup guide. Full operation needs DaVinci Resolve and a local media library.
projects.learning: Visible intermediate files make an automated pipeline editable: you can inspect and fix the plan before anything is rendered.
cv_points: Transcribes a voiceover, trims silences and filler words, writes synced captions.
Picks clips and sound, grades colour and builds a DaVinci Resolve timeline.

hackathons.title: A digital twin that finds where university heating is wasted
hackathons.summary: Our faculties spend hundreds of thousands of euros a year on heating. We proposed a sensor network that collects data over a measurement period, builds a digital twin of the buildings and uses it to find where heat is lost or spent at the wrong time.
points: Count body heat: each person in a room gives off around 100 W, so a full lecture hall can be pre-heated about 1 °C lower.
Heat by the timetable: warm a room for the classes actually scheduled in it, not on a fixed clock.
Shift heating to the night where the building can store it.
Heat only the rooms in use at a given time, not the whole building.
hackathons.cv: Sensors and a digital twin to cut faculty heating costs: body-heat-aware pre-heating, timetable-based and room-level heating.
